topics.title: Electric Charge
topics.description: The fundamental property of matter that causes electromagnetic phenomena.
objectives: Explain the nature of electric charge and its conservation
Apply Coulomb's law to compute forces between charges
Distinguish conductors from insulators
Describe charging by conduction and induction

problem_templates.prompt_template: Two point charges q₁ = +3 μC and q₂ = −5 μC are 0.2 m apart. Compute the magnitude and direction of the Coulomb force on each. Use k = 8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C².
Three charges (+2 μC, −3 μC, +4 μC) are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle with side 0.1 m. Find the net force on the +4 μC charge using vector superposition.

topics.title: Electric Field
topics.description: The vector field representing the force per unit charge at every point in space.
objectives: Define electric field as force per unit charge
Draw and interpret field lines
Compute fields from point charges and distributions
Understand superposition of electric fields

problem_templates.prompt_template: Find the electric field at a point P located 0.3 m from a +5 μC charge. Give magnitude and direction. Then find the force on a −2 μC test charge placed at P.
Two charges +q and −q are separated by distance d (an electric dipole). Find the electric field at a point on the perpendicular bisector at distance r >> d. Simplify using the dipole approximation.
A uniform line charge λ (C/m) lies along the z-axis from z = −L to z = +L. Set up but do not evaluate the integral for the electric field at a point (r, 0, 0) on the x-axis. Explain each element dE.

topics.title: Gauss's Law
topics.description: Relates total electric flux through a closed surface to the enclosed charge.
objectives: Define electric flux
State Gauss's law in integral form
Apply Gauss's law to symmetric charge distributions
Derive field inside/outside a uniformly charged sphere

problem_templates.prompt_template: A spherical shell of radius R carries total charge Q uniformly distributed. Using Gauss's law, find E(r) for (a) r < R and (b) r > R. Choose appropriate Gaussian surfaces and justify your choice.
An infinite line charge with λ = 2×10⁻⁶ C/m. Using a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length L, derive E(r). Compute E at r = 0.05 m.

A solid non-conducting sphere of radius R has volume charge density ρ(r) = ρ₀(1 − r/R). Find the total charge Q, then use Gauss's law to find E(r) for both r < R and r > R. Show the charge enclosed as a function of r.

topics.title: Electric Potential
topics.description: Potential energy per unit charge — the scalar counterpart to the electric field.
objectives: Define electric potential and potential difference (voltage)
Relate potential to electric field via the gradient
Calculate potential from point charges
Understand equipotential surfaces

problem_templates.prompt_template: Find the electric potential at a point 0.2 m from a +8 μC charge. Then compute the potential energy of a −3 μC charge placed at that point.

Two charges +4 μC (at origin) and −4 μC (at x = 0.1 m) form a dipole. Find the potential at (a) the midpoint between them and (b) a point on the perpendicular bisector 0.05 m away. Interpret the results.
Given V(x,y) = 3x² − 2y² (volts), find the electric field vector E = −∇V. Identify the equipotential surfaces and sketch a few field lines.

topics.title: DC Circuits
topics.description: Analysis of direct-current circuits using Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's rules.
objectives: Apply Ohm's law V=IR
Analyze series and parallel resistor networks
Apply Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws
Compute power dissipation in resistors

problem_templates.prompt_template: Three resistors (4Ω, 6Ω, 12Ω) are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. Find the equivalent resistance, total current, and current through each resistor.
A circuit has two loops with battery E₁ = 12 V (R₁ = 3Ω in series), battery E₂ = 8 V (R₂ = 2Ω in series), and shared R₃ = 4Ω. Apply Kirchhoff's laws to find the current in each branch.
Find the Thevenin equivalent of a circuit with a 24 V source, R₁ = 6Ω in series, and R₂ = 12Ω in parallel with the output terminals. Compute V_th and R_th. Then find the current through a 4Ω load.

topics.title: Magnetism
topics.description: Magnetic forces, fields, and the behavior of moving charges in magnetic fields.
objectives: Describe magnetic force on moving charges (Lorentz force)
Compute magnetic field from current-carrying wires
Apply the right-hand rule
Understand magnetic dipoles and bar magnets

problem_templates.prompt_template: A proton (q = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, m = 1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg) moves at 3×10⁶ m/s in the +x direction through B = 0.2 T in the +z direction. Find the magnetic force vector and the radius of the resulting circular orbit.

An infinite straight wire carries current I = 5 A. Find the magnetic field at distance r = 0.1 m using Ampere's law. Then find the force per meter on a parallel wire carrying I = 3 A at the same distance.

A rectangular current loop (a × b, current I) is placed in a uniform field B parallel to the loop plane. Derive the torque on the loop and show it equals τ = m × B where m is the magnetic dipole moment.

topics.title: Faraday's Law and Induction
topics.description: A changing magnetic flux induces an EMF — the foundation of generators and transformers.
objectives: State Faraday's law of induction
Apply Lenz's law to determine direction of induced current
Compute induced EMF for moving conductors
Understand mutual and self-inductance

problem_templates.prompt_template: A circular loop of radius 0.1 m is in a magnetic field B = 0.5 sin(100πt) T perpendicular to the loop. Find the induced EMF as a function of time. Use Faraday's law and Lenz's law.

A conducting rod of length 0.5 m moves at 2 m/s perpendicular to B = 0.3 T. Find the induced EMF, and if the rod has resistance 2Ω in a closed loop of total resistance 5Ω, find the induced current and the power dissipated.

An ideal transformer has N₁ = 200 turns and N₂ = 50 turns. The primary voltage is 240 V AC. Find the secondary voltage and current if a 10Ω load is attached. Verify power conservation. Explain how this relies on Faraday's law.
